metric_rationale: In all 8 trials of this design, the single most valid discriminating cue always favors Option A. Thus, Take The Best (TTB) will consistently choose Option A, resulting in a mean response close to 0. In contrast, the trials are designed with a compensatory structure where Option B has a larger number of slightly less valid cues, such that their sum outweighs Option A's single best cue in most trials (6 out of 8). Therefore, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model will consistently choose Option B in those trials, resulting in an overall mean response closer to 0.75. Simply computing the overall proportion of times Option B was chosen (response == 1) perfectly discriminates the two theories.

By design, the first discriminating cue in every trial favors Option A. Thus, TTB predicts a constant, high probability of choosing Option A across all trials, regardless of the values of the remaining cues. In contrast, WADD integrates all cues, so its preference for Option A will strongly depend on the net difference in the number of positive features between the options. This metric computes the difference in the rate of choosing Option A between trials where Option A has more positive features overall than Option B, and trials where Option A has fewer positive features. TTB predicts this difference to be near zero, whereas WADD predicts a large positive difference.

This metric calculates the proportion of trials in which the subject's choice matches the prediction of the Take The Best (TTB) model. In the provided experimental design, TTB and Tallying make strictly opposing predictions on several trials, and Tallying is forced to guess on others where TTB makes a deterministic choice. Therefore, data simulated under TTB will yield a high TTB-match proportion (near 1, subject to noise), while data simulated under Tallying will yield a very low TTB-match proportion (below 0.5, because it actively chooses the opposite on many trials and guesses on the rest).

In all trials, Option A possesses the highest validity cue while Option B does not. Therefore, Take The Best (TTB) will deterministically favor Option A across all trials, meaning its choice probability should remain constant regardless of the total number of features each option has. In contrast, Tallying bases decisions on the difference in the total number of positive features. This metric computes the absolute difference in the mean response rate between trials where Option B has more features (diff < 0) and trials where Option A has more features (diff > 0). The absolute difference is calculated per subject to prevent cancellation from subjects with negative Tallying weights, and then averaged. Tallying will produce a large absolute difference, while TTB will produce a difference near zero.

This metric evaluates the difference in choice confidence (accuracy in choosing the top-cue favored option) when the single discriminating cue is the 1st ranked cue versus when it is the 4th or 5th ranked cue. Take The Best assigns a binary score of 1 vs 0 as long as any cue discriminates, predicting absolutely zero drop in accuracy as the discriminating cue moves down the hierarchy. In contrast, Rank-Weighted Additive scales features by an inverse power of their rank, so the score difference is drastically smaller when the 4th or 5th cue is the first to discriminate, predicting a sharp drop in accuracy towards 50/50.

In the Rank-Weighted Additive (WADD) model, cue weights are determined by an inverse power function of their rank (1/rank^gamma). When Option A's best cue is Cue 1, its weight is 1.0, leading to a large score difference and a deterministic choice for A. However, when Option A relies on Cue 2 or 3 (Trials 10-16), the weights exponentially decay if gamma is large. This severely compresses the score difference between A and B, causing the softmax function to produce near-random guessing (or even favor B if gamma is small and B has multiple cues). In contrast, Take The Best (TTB) assigns a binary score (1.0 for the winner, 0.0 for the loser) based purely on the first discriminating cue, entirely avoiding this score compression. TTB therefore predicts a high, consistent probability of choosing Option A across all trials. By subtracting the rate of choosing A on trials where A lacks Cue 1 from trials where A has Cue 1, we obtain a metric that is near zero for TTB but strongly positive for WADD.

Calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice matches the prediction of the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. Under TTB, subjects base their decision purely on the first discriminating cue, leading to a high match rate. Under the competing random guessing theory, subjects have a constant bias for one option over the other; because exactly half the experimental trials favor Option A under TTB and half favor Option B, any constant bias will yield a TTB match rate of exactly 0.5 on average. This creates a large and highly reliable gap between the two theories.

Calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice matches the prediction of the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. Because the experimental design consists entirely of exact mirror-image stimulus pairs, the Random Guessing model (which relies on a fixed positional bias) will agree with TTB exactly 50% of the time on average, with very low variance. In contrast, the TTB model will systematically agree with its own predictions at a rate substantially higher than 50%.
